newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Sydney air traffic to double in 13 yrs -study.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Sydney air traffic to double in 13 yrs -study.

text.p: Airline traffic moving through Sydney will double in 13 years, showing that the city needed a second big airport, not the small overflow operation previously planned, the government said on Wednesday.
By the end of next decade, 40.4 million passengers would use the airport per year, compared with 20.3 million in the year to June 1996, Transport Minister John Sharp said in a statement.
"The projected substantial high growth rates in aviation activity in the Sydney basin highlighted the need for a second major airport," he said.
The second airport would initially take less traffic than the current airport, in the suburb of Mascot, but would grow in importance.
"I don't envisage the second airport will be the major airport," Sharp said.
"For historic and economic reasons, Mascot will still be the major airport, simply because that's where the two major airlines have got their facilities."
"But the importance and significance of the second airport will grow as the amount of traffic grows and the increase in traffic is steered towards the second airport."
The new airport would be able to handle 360,000 take-offs and landings a year, compared with the current 270,000 at Mascot and the projected 426,000 at the end of next decade.

Airport plans for Sydney are being driven by noise as well as economics and Sharp also issued an operating plan for Sydney airport proposed by regulator Airservices Australia to shift aircraft away from houses.
The plan would move more of the airport's take-offs and landings over Botany Bay, which lies to the south of the terminals, rather than the suburbs to the north, east and west.
Mascot is just a 20 minute taxi ride from the city centre, which makes it as convenient for travellers as it is inconvenient for residents.

The former Labor government, ousted by the Liberal-Nationals in last year's election, approved a third runway for Sydney in the late 1980s but also planned a new airport at Badgerys Creek, which is at least an hour's drive from the city and lacks rail links.
But Sharp is looking at a much closer site at Holsworthy, a former army firing range previously ruled out in part because of the presence of unexploded ammunition.
The government says new technology can economically clean up the site, which also has a freeway nearby and a rail line to the city running straight through it.
Sharp said he wants the new airport to take much of the air traffic load for Sydney, rather than just overflow operations such as light aircraft and freight.
The latest traffic forecasts were significantly above those projected in 1985 when Labor drew up its plans, he said.

"This is largely because earlier forecasts underestimated the high growth rates associated with deregulation of domestic aviation and rapid development of Australia's international aviation traffic, which is expected to grow at an average annual rate of nearly nine percent to the year 2000 and nearly seven percent to the year 2010."
By comparison, worldwide international passenger growth was expected to be five percent a year.
